Module 4: Ethical Data Visualization

Introduction

Data visualizations play a powerful role in managerial communication. Well-designed charts help decision makers quickly identify patterns, compare alternatives, and understand complex information. However, the same visual tools that clarify information can also distort it.

Misleading visualizations do not always involve incorrect data. In many cases, the numbers themselves are accurate, but the way they are displayed influences interpretation. Small design choices (e.g., axis scaling, chart type, or selective framing) can significantly affect how viewers perceive the data.2Stobierski, T. (2021). Bad data visualization: Examples of misleading data. Harvard Business School Online. 6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders.

For managers and analysts, understanding these risks is essential. Ethical visualization requires more than technical accuracy; it requires responsible communication. Charts should represent the underlying data faithfully and avoid design choices that exaggerate patterns or hide important context.6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders.

This module examines common ways visualizations can mislead viewers and introduces principles for evaluating the ethical implications of visual framing.

Why Ethical Visualization Matters

Managers often rely on visualizations to support decisions involving strategy, operations, and investments. Because visualizations simplify complex information, they can influence interpretation more strongly than tables of numbers.

Research on graphical perception shows that viewers frequently interpret charts visually before reading labels or values.1Cleveland, W. S., & McGill, R. (1984). Graphical perception: Theory, experimentation, and application to the development of graphical methods. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 79(387), 531–554. As a result, design choices can shape conclusions even when the underlying data are accurate. For example:

  • A chart with a truncated axis may exaggerate differences.
  • A chart on dual axes may compress or exaggerate perceived relationships depending on how the axes are scaled.
  • A visualization that omits historical context (i.e., cherry picking) may suggest trends that are not meaningful.
  • A chart comparing two variables may imply causation even when only correlation exists.

These issues highlight an important responsibility for analysts and managers: Visualizations should clarify reality, not manipulate perception. Ethical visualization ensures that charts inform decisions without biasing interpretation through distortion.6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders.

Truncated Axes

One of the most common sources of misleading charts is the use of truncated axes.2Stobierski, T. (2021). Bad data visualization: Examples of misleading data. Harvard Business School Online. 3Dougherty, J., & Ilyankou, I. (2021). How to lie with charts. Hands-On Data Visualization. A truncated axis occurs when the vertical axis of a bar or column chart does not begin at zero. When the axis starts at a higher value, small differences between bars appear much larger than they actually are.

Because bar charts encode values through length, starting the axis above zero distorts the visual representation of magnitude.1Cleveland, W. S., & McGill, R. (1984). Graphical perception: Theory, experimentation, and application to the development of graphical methods. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 79(387), 531–554. 4Datawrapper Academy. (2021). Why our column and bar charts start at zero (or below). For this reason, many visualization guidelines recommend that bar charts should start at zero unless there is a compelling analytical justification.

Such charts are sometimes used unintentionally because spreadsheet software automatically adjusts axes to fit the data. However, they can also be used strategically to influence perception. This example illustrates how visualizations can shape interpretation even when the underlying numbers are accurate.

Effective and ethical visualization requires designers to ask an important question: Does this chart represent the data fairly, or does the design exaggerate the story?

The article “Why Bars Start at Zero” explains that failing to do so can lead viewers to overestimate differences between values.4Datawrapper Academy. (2021). Why our column and bar charts start at zero (or below). However, truncated axes are not always inappropriate. In some cases, particularly when analyzing small differences, you may choose to zoom in on a range of values. When doing so, the chart should clearly indicate the truncated scale and explain the reason for the design choice.5Few, S. (2012). Show me the numbers: Designing tables and graphs to enlighten (2nd ed.). Analytics Press.

In managerial contexts, misleading visualizations can lead to poor decisions, damage trust with decision makers, and even harm your reputation and credibility.

The Misleading Effect of Truncated Axes in Bar Charts

Let us consider a chart comparing company revenue between two years: 2024 = $100M and 2025 = $105M. The examples below demonstrate the effect of a truncated y-axis.

Note: These charts show the effect of truncated axes. Since the y-axis begins at $95 million rather than zero, the difference between the bars appears impressive. The chart may visually suggest explosive growth, even though the actual increase is modest. When we compare that chart to another one with the same values and appropriate scale, we can see that actual increase represents only a 5% change, which is meaningful but not dramatic.

Dual Axes

Another visualization technique that can create confusion is the use of dual axes, where two different vertical scales appear on the same chart.5Few, S. (2012). Show me the numbers: Designing tables and graphs to enlighten (2nd ed.). Analytics Press. Dual-axis charts are often used when comparing two variables that have different units or magnitudes, such as:

  • sales revenue and advertising spending
  • temperature and energy consumption

While this approach may appear convenient, it can produce misleading patterns.

Because each variable uses a different scale, it is possible to manipulate the axes so that the lines appear to move together, even when the underlying data do not show a meaningful relationship.3Dougherty, J., & Ilyankou, I. (2021). How to lie with charts. Hands-On Data Visualization. For example, adjusting the axis ranges can make two unrelated variables appear strongly correlated.

Visualization experts frequently recommend avoiding dual-axis charts when possible. Instead, analysts may use:

  • separate charts
  • indexed charts
  • normalized values

These alternatives allow viewers to compare trends without introducing scale distortions.5Few, S. (2012). Show me the numbers: Designing tables and graphs to enlighten (2nd ed.). Analytics Press.

Dual-axis and single-axis charts compare GDP of the world vs. the United States using real data from the World Bank. Is it fair to make a comparison using different scales? What happens if we remove one axis and put both series on the same scale?

In the first figure, the United States series uses a different y-axis than the world series, making the two lines look more similar than they really are; the misleading effect of the dual axes is revealed when both series are plotted on the same scale.

Cherry-Picking and Context Manipulation

Another way visualizations can mislead viewers is through selective presentation of data.2Stobierski, T. (2021). Bad data visualization: Examples of misleading data. Harvard Business School Online. 3Dougherty, J., & Ilyankou, I. (2021). How to lie with charts. Hands-On Data Visualization. Cherry-picking occurs when analysts display only a subset of the data that supports a particular narrative. For example, a chart may show sales growth over the past three months while ignoring a longer trend that reveals declining performance over the past year.

Similarly, visualizations may omit contextual information that would change interpretation. For instance, a chart showing a sharp increase in revenue may appear impressive until viewers learn that the increase occurred after a period of unusually low sales.

In both cases, the visualization may be technically accurate but misleading due to incomplete context. Ethical visualization requires us to consider whether the chart fairly represents the broader dataset.6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders.

Cherry-Picking Data is Data Manipulation

Ethical data visualization isn't just about avoiding "fake" numbers; it is about transparency in presentation. Choosing a narrow window of time can intentionally or unintentionally bias interpretation; ethical visualizations aim to inform decisions rather than distort them.

Note: These examples demonstrate how easily viewers can be misled when a narrow slice of data is presented without appropriate context. Always ask, "Does this window represent the broader trend or just one moment?" If the meaning of your visualization changes substantially when you zoom out, the original framing may be misleading.

Correlation vs. Causation

Visualizations are frequently used to illustrate relationships between variables. However, viewers often interpret these relationships as causal even when no causal link exists.6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders. For example, a scatter plot may show a strong relationship between two variables, such as:

  • ice cream sales and drowning incidents (See Figure 4-7)
  • advertising spending and revenue

While these variables may move together, the relationship may be driven by other factors. In the case of ice cream sales and drowning incidents, both variables increase during warmer months. The apparent relationship arises from seasonal effects, not a causal connection between the two variables. In statistical terms, we refer to those events as spurious correlations.6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders.

Even when visualizations show relationships between variables for which a clear connection has been established, the presenter should be careful to avoid language or design choices that imply causation without supporting evidence. Visualizations depict statistical relationships (associations) from observational data such as how they change together rather than the underlying mechanism of why they change.6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders.

For data visualization, report the correlation coefficient (r) to show the direction (positive or negative) and strength of a relationship, but report R2 (coefficient of determination) to explain how well a model fits the data.

To compute a correlation, use the =CORREL(array1, array2) function for a single coefficient, or the Data Analysis ToolPak (Data > Data Analysis > Correlation) to generate a matrix for multiple variables.

See the "How-To" section in the module for a practical example.

Visual Framing and Interpretation

Visual framing refers to the way design choices shape how viewers interpret data.6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders. Framing can occur through several mechanisms, including:

  • highlighting certain data points
  • choosing specific time ranges
  • emphasizing particular comparisons

For example, a chart comparing quarterly profits might highlight a recent increase while minimizing the longer-term trend. While framing is an unavoidable aspect of communication, ethical visualization requires transparency about how the data are presented.6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders. Managers should consider whether the visualization supports an objective understanding of the data or encourages a particular interpretation.

Ethical Data Visualization Goes Beyond Plotting Data on a Chart

Let us consider a scenario where we are trying to evaluate the effect of our newly deployed AI agents on customer satisfaction by examining whether the total time customers spend with AI agents relates to customer satisfaction. After plotting the data on the first chart, we may think that time spent with the agent makes no difference on customer satisfaction since customers are either very satisfied or very dissatisfied if they spend 0 to 5 minutes with the agent. Ethical visualization requires us to frame the data to help the viewer interpret the data correctly.6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders. In the second figure, we can see that if we present the data segmented by color, two very clear patterns emerge.

Note: When all cases are viewed together, the relationship between interaction time and satisfaction appears inconsistent. However, when segmenting the data into two distinct groups: resolved cases, where shorter interaction times are generally associated with higher satisfaction, and unresolved cases, which cluster at low satisfaction regardless of time. This illustrates the importance of segmenting data before drawing conclusions. The toolkit included in the module provides the dataset and details how you can replicate the plots, analyze them, and report the findings.

Evaluating Visualization Ethics

When evaluating a chart, managers should consider several questions:5Few, S. (2012). Show me the numbers: Designing tables and graphs to enlighten (2nd ed.). Analytics Press. 6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders.

  • Does the visualization represent the magnitude of the data accurately?
  • Are important contextual details missing?
  • Does the design exaggerate patterns or relationships?
  • Could viewers reasonably misinterpret the chart?

Answering these questions helps ensure that visualizations support clear and responsible decision making.6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders.

Ethical visualization is not simply about avoiding deception; it is about designing charts that allow viewers to understand the data as faithfully as possible.6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders.

Examples of Manipulating the Axis Scale and the Values in a Visualization

One common way charts can mislead viewers is through axis manipulation, particularly when the vertical axis does not start at zero.2Stobierski, T. (2021). Bad data visualization: Examples of misleading data. Harvard Business School Online. 4Datawrapper Academy. (2021). Why our column and bar charts start at zero (or below). Truncated axes can exaggerate small differences and create the impression of dramatic change.

A widely discussed example appeared on Fox News in 2012, where a bar chart compared the tax top rate at the time to what it would be if the tax cuts of the Bush administration were allowed to expire. The chart used a vertical axis that began around 34% instead of 0%, causing a relatively small change in the top tax rate to appear much larger than it actually was.2Stobierski, T. (2021). Bad data visualization: Examples of misleading data. Harvard Business School Online. 4Datawrapper Academy. (2021). Why our column and bar charts start at zero (or below). While a change from 35% to 39.6% in the tax rate may represent only a modest difference in mathematical terms, when the axis begins at 34%, the bars appear dramatically different in height, visually amplifying the change.

Note: The chart on the left is from a 2012 Fox News broadcast and uses a truncated vertical axis, which exaggerates the difference between 35% and 39.6%. The chart on the right presents the same data using a zero-based axis, showing the change proportionally.

Another very well-known example also appeared on Fox News in 2011 where a line chart was used to show changes in the monthly unemployment rate during Obama’s presidency. The chart used a vertical axis that began around 8% instead of 0%, which in this case is not as problematic as the previous example, since we are tracking changes over time, and even small changes in unemployment are important. However, aside from the scaling issue, the graph was manipulated. If you notice, the graph does not show any change from October to November despite the different values. If those values are plotted correctly, we can see a clear drop in the unemployment rate over time.

Note: The chart on the left is from Fox News broadcast in 2011; the chart shows a truncated axis and inaccurately plotted values, obscuring the drop from 9.0% to 8.6%. On the right, the same data was plotted accurately, clearly showing the decline in unemployment.

As you can see, the issue is not necessarily that truncated axes are always inappropriate. In some contexts, especially when analyzing small differences between values, a truncated axis may be justified. The ethical concern arises when the chart fails to clearly indicate the truncated scale or when the design appears intended to exaggerate differences, or when the visualization is manipulated.

This example highlights an important principle of ethical visualization: Design choices should not distort the magnitude of the data. When presenting information to decision makers, you should consider how viewers will interpret the chart visually, not just numerically.

Both visualizations could technically present correct data, yet still mislead viewers. An ethical visualization would show the full-time range, use an appropriate axis scale, and clearly label the chart. This approach ensures that stakeholders interpret the data accurately.

Key Takeaways

  • Visualization design can significantly influence how viewers interpret data.
  • Common sources of misleading visualizations include truncated axes, dual-axis charts, selective context, and visual representations that imply causation without supporting evidence.
  • Ethical visualization requires analysts to consider how design choices affect interpretation.
  • Managers who understand these issues are better equipped to evaluate the charts they encounter in reports, dashboards, and presentations.
  • Ultimately, effective visualization supports accurate understanding, transparent communication, and sound decision making.

Managerial Insight

Visualizations can influence how decision makers interpret data. Small design choices, such as truncated axes, selective time ranges, or dual-axis charts, can dramatically change how a trend or comparison appears.

While some misleading visuals are created intentionally, many occur because analysts or managers do not fully understand how design choices affect interpretation. In high-stakes environments such as finance, healthcare, and public policy, these misinterpretations can lead to poor decisions.

Managers therefore have a responsibility to critically evaluate the visuals presented to them.6Cairo, A. (2016). The truthful art: Data, charts, and maps for communication. New Riders. Asking questions such as “What is the full context of this data?” or “Would the trend look the same if the axis started at zero?” helps ensure that decisions are based on accurate and ethical representations of the evidence.
